factors.factor: Architecture with a single primary and a standby used only for failover meant all load fell on one database, increasing susceptibility to load spikes and replication lag.
factors.evidence: "In this setup a single database has to handle all the load, which is not ideal."

factors.factor: Replication lag caused WAL segments needed by the secondary to be removed from the primary, and without WAL archiving the secondary could only be resynchronised manually
factors.evidence: "The replication failed as WAL segments needed by the secondary were already removed from the primary. As GitLab.com was not using WAL archiving, the secondary had to be re-synchronised manually."

factors.factor: Increased database load from suspected spam and a background job hard-deleting an account flagged for abuse (accidentally scheduled for removal) compounded the replication problem.
factors.evidence: "GitLab.com starts experiencing an increase in database load due to what we suspect was spam... part of the load was caused by a background job trying to remove a GitLab employee and their associated data."

factors.factor: Undocumented pg_basebackup behaviour (silent waiting is normal) led to the stall being interpreted as a fault, prolonging troubleshooting and prompting further destructive attempts.
factors.evidence: "this is normal behaviour: pg_basebackup will wait for the primary to start sending over replication data and it will sit and wait silently until that time. Unfortunately this was not clearly documented in our engineering runbooks nor in the official pg_basebackup document."

factors.factor: Lack of safeguards against running destructive commands on the wrong host allowed a data directory wipe intended for the secondary to be executed on the primary.
factors.evidence: "Trying to restore the replication process, an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary. Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead."

factors.factor: Backup procedure was not verified; pg_dump version selection depended on the presence of a local data directory, causing the wrong client version to be used on application servers
factors.evidence: "the backup procedure was using pg_dump 9.2, while our database is running PostgreSQL 9.6... As a result there is no PostgreSQL data directory present on these servers, thus Omnibus defaults to PostgreSQL 9.2." | "Hoping they could restore the database the engineers involved went to look for the database backups, and asked for help on Slack. Unfortunately the process of both finding and using backups failed completely."

factors.factor: Backup failure notifications were silently lost because cronjob emails were rejected by DMARC, so failures went unnoticed
factors.evidence: "these notifications are sent by email... DMARC was not enabled for the cronjob emails, resulting in them being rejected by the receiver. This means we were never aware of the backups failing, until it was too late."

factors.factor: Disaster recovery relied on mechanisms that were unsuitable or not enabled for databases: Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database servers, and LVM snapshots were not designed for disaster recovery.
factors.evidence: "While enabled for the NFS servers, these snapshots were not enabled for any of the database servers as we assumed that our other backup procedures were sufficient enough." and "the produced snapshots are not really meant to be used for disaster recovery."

factors.factor: Recovery was slowed by slow, throttled storage in staging (Azure classic without premium storage) chosen to save costs
factors.evidence: "These disks are network disks and are throttled to a really low number (around 60Mbps)... the bottleneck was in the drives."

factors.factor: Production configuration drift: max_connections set to 8000 for nearly a year, which caused semaphore limits to block PostgreSQL restart when max_wal_senders was raised
factors.evidence: "In our case this was set to 8000. Such a value is way too high, yet it had been applied almost a year ago and was working fine until that point."

action_items.action: Enable WAL archiving (continuous archiving to object storage) for the production PostgreSQL primary so replicas can catch up without manual re-synchronisation after falling behind.
Verify and fix the pg_dump backup procedure so the client binary version always matches the production PostgreSQL major version, decoupled from the presence of a local data directory.
Add automated restore tests that regularly restore the latest backup into a scratch environment and verify row counts and integrity, failing loudly if backups are missing or empty.
Configure backup and cronjob failure alerts to use a delivery path that passes DMARC (or a non-email alerting channel) and add alerting on the absence of new backup objects in the S3 bucket.
Enable Azure disk snapshots for all production database servers and document the expected restore time from each storage account location.

Add guardrails to destructive database operations, such as requiring explicit confirmation of hostname/role and a safe-mode wrapper that refuses to remove data directories on a host reporting primary role.
Update engineering runbooks to document that pg_basebackup waits silently for the primary to begin streaming, including expected output and how to verify progress from the primary side.
Review and correct production PostgreSQL configuration, including max_connections, against kernel semaphore limits, and add a configuration audit to detect values that would block restarts.
Change the background account-removal job used for spam handling to soft-delete accounts and rate-limit bulk data removal to avoid large database load spikes.
Introduce read-load distribution (e.g., connection pooling and read replicas via pgpool-II or equivalent) to reduce dependence on a single primary database.
Document a disaster recovery runbook with an explicit restore order, validated restore options, and designated decision-makers so engineers are not searching for backups under pressure.
Use premium or equivalently performant storage for staging or dedicated recovery hosts where restoration speed matters, and measure restore throughput as part of DR testing.
Add host identity indicators (for example, prominent role labels in shell prompts and tooling) to reduce the chance of running destructive commands on the wrong server.
